chapter_theme: Idaikkadar, the cowherd Siddhar, turns the pillaitamil's addresses to creatures into a yoga teaching: he scolds his own petty knowledge for drowning with the true lamp inside it, tells the dragonfly, the cuckoo and the peacock to proclaim the attainments already won (ignorance gone, egoity shed, the five senses subdued, the void seen), gives the simple swan six similes for how knowledge clears the mind and the soul is made to shine, and begins the flute songs in which release is the end of birth and silence its state. The claims are of a finished man, and the practice behind them is inward: the mind held still, the senses penned, devotion and renunciation set above household life.
structure_note: 1807 to 1809 end the address to knowledge (அறிவோடு கிளத்தல்); 1810 to 1815 are kannis to the dragonfly (தும்பீபற), each line a claim of attainment; 1816 to 1819 address the cuckoo, 1820 to 1822 the peacock, 1823 to 1828 the swan (each a simile with the lesson in the second line); 1829 to 1831 open the flute songs (புல்லாங்குழலூதல்), which continue into chapter 95. The sections follow the stock forms of the pillaitamil and the kummi, with the refrain carrying the form and the stanza carrying the sense.

1807.reading: Like a man who carries a hand-lamp and jumps into the sea, why do you sink, petty knowledge, when the true lamp is inside you?
1807.nuance: The hand-lamp is outward learning or ritual light, useless in the sea it is carried into; மெய்விளக்கு, the true lamp, is the inner light. The poet addresses his own understanding as புல்லறிவு throughout this section, so the scolding is self-directed.

1808.reading: When the shining way that is higher than the breath is within you, is the higher goal, if you only think, so hard for you, petty knowledge?
1808.nuance: வாசி is the Siddhars' word for the breath as practice (and for the horse); வாசிக்கு மேலான வாள்கதி, the bright state above the breath, sets the goal beyond even breath-yoga, as tradition takes it. வாள் may be brightness or a sword, and கதி the way or the goal; the plain sense is that what is sought is already inside.

1809.reading: See the Primal One who guards every life with love as a mother does, petty knowledge, and gain release.
1809.nuance: முன்னவன், the one before all, is the poet's name for the Lord here; the mother image makes his care impartial (எவ்வுயிரும், every life), and release follows from seeing him, not from any rite.

1810.reading: Fly, dragonfly, and say that ignorance has gone, that we have seen supreme bliss, that true knowledge has come to hand and that we have climbed up above.
1810.nuance: The dragonfly kannis (1810 to 1815) are a list of attainments in the perfect tense, each in the first person plural; the form is boast as teaching. பர மேலேறிக் கொண்டோம் (we have mounted above) can be the ascent of the breath to the crown or simply rising above the world.

1811.reading: Fly, dragonfly, and say that the net of affliction is no more, that we have shed the full load of egoity, that old karma has left and that we have seen the supreme light.
1811.nuance: ஆணவங்கள் is the Siddhanta term for the first of the three malas, the soul's self-darkness, though the plural and the plain sense allow 'prides'. The verse pairs the loss of egoity and karma with the sight of the light, as cause and effect.

1812.reading: Fly, dragonfly, and say that the five senses have been subdued, that full knowledge alone is the real, that the true things have come to us and that we have seen a divinity.
1812.nuance: அறிவே பொருள் makes knowledge itself the substance that is sought, a Siddhar commonplace; செம்பொருள்கள், the true things, is plural and unexplained, perhaps the truths of the tradition, perhaps the goods gained.

1813.reading: Fly, dragonfly, and say that we have left the three desires, that the state of supreme release is itself the attainment, that we have set our desire on God and that we have done away with this world.
1813.nuance: The three desires are the stock triad of land, gold and women. முத்தி நிலை சித்தி turns the Siddhar word for powers toward release: the only siddhi worth the name is mukti. தேவாசை keeps one desire, for God, after the three are gone.

1814.reading: Fly, dragonfly, and say that we have looked to the void expanse and lost our hold on maya, that we have reached our dwelling place and joined the state of the full and bounteous one.
1814.nuance: பாழ்வெளி, the void expanse, is Tirumular's பாழ் and the Siddhars' open space, seen as the goal rather than feared as nothing. வள்ளல்நிலை, the state of the giver, is the Lord's state; நிறை (fullness) qualifies it, so the void and the fullness are the same place.

1815.reading: Fly, dragonfly, and say that every thing is a dream, that all the world will perish, that the body is a letter written on water and that only the First is without end.
1815.nuance: அப்பில் எழுத்து, writing on water, is the verse's own image for the body's impermanence; the gloss confirms அப்பு as water. The stanza sets three perishables against one imperishable, ஆதி, and that contrast is the whole argument.

1816.reading: Call out in full joy, cuckoo, that the four inner instruments have been subdued, that the evil six beginning with lust have been contained, and that we have seen the four feet.
1816.nuance: கரணங்கள் நான்கு are mind, intellect, will and ego in Siddhanta reckoning; காமமுதல் ஓராறு the six enemies (lust, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy). சரணங்கள் ஒருநான்கு is unclear: the Lord's feet, the four paths (சரியை to ஞானம்) or four refuges have all been proposed, and I cannot fix it.

1817.reading: Say, cuckoo, that the world is a thing to retch at, that our Noble One is hard to see, that the many religions are falsehood and that we have gone past the seven births.
1817.nuance: ஒக்காளம் is vomit, the poet's physical word for disgust with the world, repeated at 1843. பலமதம் பொய்மை rejects the sects wholesale, as Tirumular's அறுசமயப் பிணக்கம் does; எழு பவம், the seven births, is the stock count of the cycle.

1818.reading: Say, cuckoo, that those who perform the practices will die and those who have mastered all the tattvas will burn, that a fruit like that of great austerities will not come, and that only the root mantras bring greatness.
1818.nuance: A hard verse: சாதனங்கள், the practices, and தத்துவங்கள், the tattvas, are dismissed in favour of மூல மந்திரங்கள், the root mantras, which tradition takes as the seed syllables and the five letters. வேவார் may be 'will be scorched' or 'will suffer'; மாதவங்கள் போலும் பலன் வாயா (the gloss gives வாயா as 'will not accrue') is read as the fruit of great tapas not coming either. 1855 tells the herdsman to hold fast to the practices, so the dismissal here is of practice without the mantra, on one reading.

1819.reading: Say, cuckoo, that those who know the eight and the two have no trouble, that if the mind stands without straying one reaches the goal; know it by coming close to the play, and sing with the Primal Lord in your thought.
1819.nuance: எட்டிரண்டு is Siddhar cipher: tradition reads the Tamil numerals for eight (௮) and two (௨) as the letters அ and உ, the first two sounds of Om and the sun and moon breaths; the plain sum is ten, or eight twos, sixteen. நட்டணை is glossed as acting or performance, perhaps the Lord's dance, perhaps the world's show; the line is obscure.

1820.reading: Dance, peacock, dance, having seen our Primal One adorned with the serpent; before the cage goes, take the way, and take the path of silence without ever failing.
1820.nuance: ஆதியணி சேடன் is read as the Primal One who wears the serpent (Siva), though அணிசேடன் could be Adisesha himself. கூடு, the cage or nest, is the body; the urgency is that the way must be taken before death, and the way named is மோனநெறி, silence.

1821.reading: Dance, peacock, saying that household life is affliction and that for those without devotion there is neither release nor attainment; see that the good dharma is the dharma of renunciation, and seek the pure open space at the end of sound.
1821.nuance: The verse ranks the two dharmas flatly, இல்லறம் as sorrow and துறவறம் as the good, and adds a second condition, பத்தி, without which no attainment comes. நாதாந்த வெட்டவெளி, the open space beyond nada, is one of Tirumular's six ends (ஆறந்தம்), the place where sound itself ceases.

1822.reading: Show the mind to be like a body of wind, peacock; drive Death far off when he comes; leap so as to pass through the milk-way; and make the mind without the least inward clinging.
1822.nuance: காற்றூனை and பாற்றூடு are both obscure and may be corrupt. Tradition reads காற்று ஊன் as the mind made as light as breath, and பால் ஊடு as passing through the milk, the nectar of the head that the milking songs (1840 to 1845) are about; plainly the lines are a peacock's flight and a leap through a stream. The clear part is the last line, no inner attachment.

1823.reading: If a small frog stirs the water, the reflection of a picture is lost; so, simple swan, if one stirs the other mouth, the understanding is confused.
1823.nuance: The swan verses are each one simile. Still water showing an image is the still mind; the frog is the small disturbance that ruins it. மறுவாய் is unclear: the second opening, the mouth of blemish, or speech itself; மதி is both intellect and the moon, which the tradition places in the head, so the stirred moon is also the lost nectar.

1824.reading: As a tree is broken in the wind, simple swan, so if good knowledge blows, ignorance goes far away.
1824.nuance: தூற்றிவிடில் is to winnow or to scatter, so knowledge acts as the wind, not the tree; the simile makes ignorance something brittle that cannot stand once knowledge moves.

1825.reading: As a bale of cotton is destroyed by fire, simple swan, so by ripe good knowledge sin departs.
1825.nuance: பக்குவ நல் அறிவு, ripened knowledge, is the condition; the fire-and-cotton image makes the destruction total and instant. பாவம் here is the deed's stain rather than karma as a principle.

1826.reading: As a wasp brings a grub to its nest and shapes it into form, simple swan, so bring the rich, hard mind under control.
1826.nuance: The simile rests on the old belief (the பிரமரகீடம் figure) that the wasp turns the grub into a wasp by brooding over it; so the mind is remade by steady attention rather than broken. வளமுடைய வன்மனம் grants the mind both strength and richness before asking that it be mastered.

1827.reading: As salt put into water becomes one with it, in the same measure, simple swan, so stand fittingly united with Brahman.
1827.nuance: அளவு சரியானது, becoming equal in measure, is the point of the simile: the salt does not vanish but is everywhere in the water. The union named is with பிரமம், the Vedantic word, where the rest of the work says சிவம் or பரம்.

1828.reading: As heated iron shows its colour, simple swan, so make the soul shine to its full and grow rich.
1828.nuance: The iron glows by the fire in it, and the soul by the practice (the heat of tapas, on the usual reading) that is applied to it; the glow is the soul's own light made visible, not something added.

1829.reading: Blow the flute, herdsman, saying that for those who have done away with the old round of birth there is no further thing called release.
1829.nuance: The flute songs (1829 to 1839) are addressed to கோன், the herdsman or king, that is the poet himself. முத்திதான் இல்லை can mean that release is nothing other than the ending of birth, so nothing remains to be gained, or, less likely, that such people do not need release; the first reading fits 1831, which places release in silence.

1830.reading: Blow the flute to the end, herdsman, saying that even if one gains the pleasures of Indra, they are trouble.
1830.nuance: இந்திர போகம் is the summit of worldly and heavenly enjoyment, and it is placed under தொல்லை, trouble, the word used of the round of birth in 1829. அந்தமாய் is either 'beautifully' or 'as the final word'.

1831.reading: Blow the flute as a song, herdsman, saying that in the state of silence release comes to be.
1831.nuance: The verse answers 1829: release is not a further thing but a state, மோன நிலை. That silence is to be proclaimed on a flute is the poem's joke and its method, for the flute is the one instrument that sounds without words.

links.note: Tirumular says the Lord is kinder than a mother to those who love well; Idaikkadar says the Primal One guards every life with love as a mother does, and release comes from seeing him. Tirumular restricts the nearness to lovers, Idaikkadar extends the care to every life.

Tirumular counts a hundred sects within six and says the supreme path is no path of theirs; Idaikkadar tells the cuckoo that the many religions are falsehood and that the Noble One is hard to see. Both reject the sects as a whole rather than one in favour of another.

Tirumular says the sages who waited for release by praise alone did not know the fruit that tattva-knowledge gives; Idaikkadar says those who have mastered all the tattvas will burn, and only the root mantras bring greatness. The conflict holds on the reading that தத்துவங்கள் தேர்ந்தவர்கள் are those who know the tattva doctrine, which Tirumular's verse prizes and Idaikkadar's dismisses.

1818 says those who perform the practices (சாதனங்கள்) will die; 1855 tells the herdsman to hold the practices well in hand and keep to them. The conflict holds if the two verses mean the same practices; it dissolves if 1818 means outward rites and 1855 the inner disciplines of the herding songs.

The Kural says a household life that keeps to virtue has more endurance than those who do penance; Idaikkadar says household life is affliction and the good dharma is renunciation. The conflict is direct on the ranking of the two dharmas, which the Kural's chapter on household life argues one way and this verse the other.

Pattinathar says that forest, rags and bowl gain nothing without inner love, and that true lovers reach the home of knowledge even staying in the house beside their women; Idaikkadar says household life is sorrow and renunciation is the good dharma. Both make devotion the condition, but they disagree on whether leaving the house is the better dharma, Pattinathar denying that the outward state decides and Idaikkadar ranking it.

Tirumular makes devotion and the knowledge that is dispassion the seed of the supreme siddhi; Idaikkadar says that without devotion there is neither release nor siddhi and that renunciation is the good dharma. The pair of conditions is the same in both.

Both use heated iron. In Tirumular the heat that stays after the fire is withdrawn is the stain of karma that lingers even in turiya, a warning; in Idaikkadar the glow of the heated iron is the soul made to shine by practice, an encouragement. The same image carries opposite lessons.

Tirumular says that for those to whom silence has come, release comes too and the powers stand before them; Idaikkadar says that in the state of silence release comes to be. Both make silence the state in which release is found rather than a vow that precedes it.

source_issues: 1810 to 1815 and 1817 print a space inside words ending in -ோம் and -ோர் (கண்டோ ம், விட்டோ ம், அகன்றிட்டோ ம், விட்டோ ர்), a transcription artefact of the ோ sign; the words are read whole.
1822 lines 1 and 3: காற்றூனைப் போல் and பாற்றூடு உருவவே are hard to construe and may be corrupt; the readings follow tradition's guess (wind-body, milk-way).
1823 line 2: மறுவாயைத் தான்கலக்கின் is obscure; no variant is given.
